GENERAL POST OFFICE BUILDING, THIRD FLOOR
250 NORTH SOOCHOW ROAD
SHANGHAI
August 9, 1937
PERSONAL
Mr. S. W. Morgan
Pan American Airways Company
New York
Dear Mr. Morgan:
I received a cable recently from Colonel Young in which
he stated that he assumed that I would keep him posted with respect
to the current crisis in China and how it might affect trans-Pacific
operations.
I can not see how any development in this section of the
world could affect our operations in Hongkong.
As you know, I have
felt all along until just recently that the Far Eastern crisis would
be averted through compromise.
It appears now, however,
as though
the demand for war among the chinese provincial leaders
is so strong
that it can no longer be ignored by Chiang Kai-shek, and that he will
be compelled in the interests of natimal unity to make some kind
of a show of resistance. Obviously, no one can guess how far such
an operation may extend, or what element it may eventually draw into
the conflict.
The best
thought in Shanghai seems to indicate that
an attack may be launched by the Chinese in the North with the an-
nounced objective of driving the Japanese from Peking and Tientsin,
but with the actual objective of satisfying Chinese public opinion
and swinging the entire populace into line where close support will
be given to the Central Government.
Certain powerful sections in the
crazy-quilt pattern of Chinese politics which have been demanding
war on Japan, else withdrawal from the Chinese Central Government,
will be given an opportunity to fight in the North.
There will be,
I suspect, a few lessons learned rather quickly which will prove
rather conclusively that China is not ready for war, and there will

Japanese out.
The main drive of the Chinese, in my opinion, will
take place in North China and all other activities will be
in the
nature of side shows.
people claim that the Japanese are interested only
in taking Hopei province with a view of tieing it on to their
Sphere of Influence in North China.
Others feel that the present
aim of the Japanese
is to extend their control as far South as the
railroad which runs from Haichow near the old mouth of the Yellow
River to Sian on the West. My personal guess is that the present
plan of the Japanese is to take only Hopei and Charhar, but this
appetite may be whetted by military success, and almost anything may
follow.
A blockade of ports along the Coast wil
include Shanghai
and Canton and will probably force us to cease operation of the
Shanghai-Canton route, but apart from this "feeder service" I can
not see any effect upon the trans-Pacific except that American mails
and passengers will probably have to proceed to Hongkong via surface
transportation. Actually our trans-Pacific business may enjoy some-
thing of a boom by reason of the disruption of transpotation, al-
though I fully expect that the Dollar Line, the Canadian Pacific,
and other lines will continue to function as at present with Japanese
supervision of cargo inspection and customs at Shanghai, also of
course, Japanese censorship of all mail.
We have been extremely busy and I am dictating this at home
Sunday morning because there is little if any opportunity to get any
work done at the office and you probably will not hear from me very
frequently from now on.
Very sincerely,
H. M. Bixby
Vice-President for China
